item.title: Apache Roller RCE Flaw CVE-2026-129448 Under Active Attack (2026)
item.description:
Attackers are exploiting a critical Apache Roller flaw that allows unauthenticated remote code execution, prompting urgent security updates.

A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score of 9.8), in Apache Roller could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server. Apache Roller is an open-source blogging platform written in Java. According to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) the flaw is being actively exploited in attacks in the wild.

The issue affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. It stems from unsafe deserialization in the platform’s XML-RPC endpoint, which processes certain data before checking whether the requester is authenticated. An attacker doesn’t need valid credentials to reach this vulnerable code path.

“Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.” reads the security notice published on the Apache mailing list. “This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected.”

The Apache project described the problem in its security notice published on the Apache mailing list:

The maintainers explained that the XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester. This order of operations is the core security problem: the application processes attacker-controlled data before establishing whether the request should be trusted.

The ASF also confirmed that the vulnerability is the same issue previously tracked as CVE-2026-82384. That earlier advisory, published in September 2026, listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. The new notice expands the affected version range to include releases from 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, making it important for administrators not to rely solely on the scope of the earlier advisory.

The project has explicitly confirmed exploitation in the wild, although it hasn’t disclosed technical details about the attacks, the threat actors involved, or the organizations being targeted.

“This issue is being actively exploited.” continues the notice.

Security researcher n0mi1k is credited with discovering the vulnerability, while Matt Raible reported it to the project. The ASF recommends upgrading to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later. This release disables the vendor extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

Organizations that can’t install the update immediately should apply one of the workarounds provided by the project. They can set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping. In either case, administrators must restart Apache Roller for the change to take effect.

The experts warn that simply disabling XML-RPC through the administration interface doesn’t fully address the problem in older releases. The vulnerable code can deserialize the request before checking that configuration setting, leaving the application exposed even when administrators believe they have turned the feature off.

The confirmed exploitation makes this more than a routine patching recommendation. Organizations running Apache Roller should identify every affected instance, check whether the XML-RPC endpoint is reachable, and prioritize the upgrade or the recommended workaround. Internet-facing systems deserve particular attention, but internal installations should not be overlooked: a server doesn’t need to be publicly accessible to become a useful target after an attacker gains access to an organization’s network.

The ASF has also warned that disabling the feature through the administration interface alone won’t protect older installations:

“Users who cannot upgrade right away should set “enabledForExtensions” to “false” in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the “/roller-services/xmlrpc” servlet mapping, and restart Roller.” concludes the advisory. “Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apache Roller)

item.title: nginx2root:AI Discovers Five Critical nginx Flaws and a Path to Root
item.description:
nginx2root exposes five critical nginx flaws and a Linux kernel bug that can lead to remote code execution and root access.

Xint Research has disclosed nginx2root, five distinct nginx vulnerabilities plus one Linux kernel bug, each with a proven exploit. The worst of the five, now tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an unauthenticated attacker run code remotely, and chaining it with the kernel bug reaches root on the host.

“This issue affects NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source configurations that use HTTP/2. When NGINX processes undisclosed traffic, the flow control window can exceed the allowed threshold, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow typically followed by an NGINX worker segmentation fault. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR. (CVE-2026-123007)” reads the advisory. “An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to crash the NGINX worker process, corrupt its memory, or potentially execute code remotely. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.”

Affected nginx versions run from 1.9.5 to 1.31.8, and the fix landed in 1.31.9. According to Zakir Durumeric, Co-Founder and CEO Censys, nearly 10M Internet services are running versions of Nginx vulnerable to the NGINX2Root CVEs.

The bug sits in nginx’s HTTP/2 flow control, and it’s been there since nginx added HTTP/2 in 2015, eleven years ago. An attacker corrupts memory in an nginx worker, leaks memory addresses, and overwrites a pointer to a cleanup function that fires when a connection closes.

“Specifically, the most severe vulnerability is in nginx HTTP/2 flow control. An unauthenticated remote attacker can corrupt memory in an nginx worker, leak memory addresses, and overwrite the pointer to a cleanup function that runs when a connection closes.” reads the advisory. “This can be used to execute commands with worker privileges and receive the output over an existing connection.”

The figures show why this issue matters beyond nginx itself. In a Shodan scan on 10 November, 98.9% of nginx servers with a known version were running a vulnerable release. Xint also found that 88.6% of Fortune 500 companies use nginx. These figures show how widespread the vulnerable versions are, not how many servers can actually be attacked. Some servers may not have HTTP/2 enabled or may already include a fix provided by their software vendor. Still, administrators have a large number of systems to check.

To move from control of an nginx worker to full root access, an attacker needs to exploit a second flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code. Xint tested this attack chain in environments running on AWS, GCP and Azure, including systems reachable through a public IP address. Luxembourg’s cybersecurity response team, CIRCL, also confirmed that exploiting the kernel flaw is necessary to gain root access. No active attacks have been reported so far, and CVE-2026-123007 was not on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at the time of writing.

The discovery story is worth pausing on. nginx has been fuzzed by the best researchers for two decades, and a pre-auth RCE in it is rare, the last known one dating to 2013.

“nginx runs roughly a third of the web and has been fuzzed and audited by the best researchers in the world for two decades. Pre-auth RCE in nginx almost never happens. The best known one is from 2013. This year every AI lab pointed models at it. Everyone figured the easy bugs were long gone.” continues the advisory. “While testing a new Xint capability ahead of ZeroDay Cloud, a Xint researcher pointed it at a slice of nginx, about 50,000 lines. He picked the target; Xint did the rest. Ninety minutes later it flagged high severity issues with reproduction steps specific enough to become a working exploit in under ten minutes.”

That first find was a human picking the target and an AI doing the digging. What came next was different: Xint folded what it learned into a general feature, not tuned to nginx, and that version found the other four critical bugs with no human guidance. One of those four was also found independently by other researchers around the same time, so Xint wasn’t working in a vacuum.

Four more flaws shipped fixes in the same release, each needing its own specific setup: a backend proxy running low on connections, a proxied server name built from variables combined with certain directives, HTTP/3 turned on, or nginx running as a mail proxy.

All five vulnerabilities have a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10, making them critical. NGINX Plus is also affected across several release lines. The fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 were released today, along with NGINX Plus versions 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1

Check exposure with a simple test: run openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against your server, and if it answers “ALPN protocol: h2,” HTTP/2 is on. If you’re behind a CDN, test the origin directly, since an origin serving only HTTP/1.1 can’t be hit through HTTP/2 even if your CDN speaks it to visitors. Update to the fixed version and restart nginx fully, because a reload alone leaves the old binary running.

If you can’t patch right away, turn off HTTP/2 on affected listeners as a stopgap. That blocks the worst flaw and one other, but not the remaining three, so it’s a bridge, not a destination. Distribution packages can carry a backported fix without changing the version string nginx -v reports, so check your vendor’s own advisory rather than trusting that number alone.

Xint says the main value of this discovery goes beyond finding these vulnerabilities. It’s about building a process that can quickly turn the next AI-driven attack, similar to ARTEX, into security detections before attackers can take advantage of it.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, nginx2root)

item.title: PHP Warns of Critical Flaws Ahead of November Security Release
item.description:
PHP will patch critical security flaws across supported versions, including a session handling bug that could allow remote code execution.

The PHP development team announced a new security release scheduled for November 19, warning that the updates will address vulnerabilities across all supported versions of the widely used server-side programming language. The highest severity rating is CRITICAL, although the project says the affected issues require unusual configurations or non-default setups.

“The PHP security team announces upcoming security releases scheduled for Thursday, 19 November 2026, between 14:00 and 14:30 UTC.” reads the announcement. “The issues rated CRITICAL require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups. Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available. Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.”

The announcement places the release within PHP’s regular four-week update cycle.

PHP hasn’t disclosed the technical details, vulnerability identifiers, or fixed version numbers ahead of publication. The maintainers say they’ll release that information alongside the patches, giving administrators a short window to identify affected systems and prepare their upgrades.

One vulnerability expected to be addressed is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw involving PHP session handling.

In October, PHP warned of a new code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115560, just two days after releasing emergency patches for the critical PHP2Shell flaws.

The vulnerability affects only a specific PHP configuration that PHP says is unlikely to be used in practice. An application must meet several conditions: it must configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, change it to php at runtime using ini_set(), and make this change before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also remain enabled.

In an advisory published on October 23, the project recommended disabling session upload progress until a fix becomes available in a regular release. The vulnerability is separate from PHP2Shell and is not fixed by the October 21 updates for PHP versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12.

The November release also comes less than a month after PHP addressed two other critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively known as PHP2Shell. Those flaws let unauthenticated attackers execute code remotely through specially crafted HTTP requests, and they received emergency patches on October 21.

For organizations running PHP-based applications, the immediate priority is to identify the runtime versions in production, review custom session configurations and prepare to deploy the new packages as soon as they’re released. Teams should also check whether their Linux distributions or long-term support providers distribute PHP security fixes independently of the upstream release schedule.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive security updates directly from the PHP project, although some Linux distributions and commercial vendors continue to provide backported patches. Organizations still running these versions should verify their vendor’s coverage rather than assume that an upstream release automatically protects their installations.

“Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.” concludes the announcement. “Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-115560)

item.title: European Commission Cyberattack: ARTEX AI Tool Suspected in Prolonged Disruption
item.description:
A cyberattack disrupted EU Commission services for over ten days. ARTEX is suspected, while investigators assess whether staff data was stolen.

A cyberattack has disrupted internal European Commission systems for more than ten days, hitting payroll, leave requests and medical reimbursements. Politico’s Brussels Playbook reports the Corporate Management Board, the Commission’s top internal crisis body, met urgently over the incident, and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed the full College of Commissioners on 18 November. An EU official told Politico the Commission believes it has contained most of the attack, while the full extent of any damage remains unclear.

Sysper, the HR platform for payslips, timesheets and leave, crashed briefly again on 18 November after access had been restored earlier in the week. MyPMO, the medical reimbursement system, came back online around the same time. JSIS, the staff health insurance portal, was still down on 19 November according to a Commission employee cited by Euronews, and translation services went offline on 17 November, prompting one official to admit to “swearing a lot.”

Pay still landed on time, according to staff Politico spoke to, even as some couldn’t submit timesheets or request leave. Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed the response to Politico: “Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

Some staff still complained the internal communication said little, and an IT reply about the Sysper problem cited a general technical issue without mentioning an attack.

CERT-EU, the cybersecurity team that protects EU institutions, detected the activity and identified ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing tool, as a possible tool used in the attack. An EU official told Politico that some threat actors misuse tools like ARTEX and have targeted the Commission. In a technical note published on 5 November, CERT-EU described ARTEX as a system that uses AI agents. An operator gives it an objective in plain language, and the software breaks it down into smaller tasks that the agents carry out using real hacking tools.

ARTEX does not include its own AI model. Instead, it connects to an external AI model selected by the operator. Its original developer removed the project from its repository in October after reports of misuse. However, independent copies are still available, so removing the original project does not prevent others from using it. So far, there is no public information explaining how the attackers entered the Commission’s systems. The reference to ARTEX therefore points to a suspected tool, not a confirmed attack method or the identity of those responsible.

The biggest unanswered question is whether staff data was stolen. This could include names, salary details, home addresses or health information. Investigators have not yet confirmed whether anyone accessed this data, which explains why the Commission has shared little information with employees.

Taking systems offline or restoring them does not prove that no data was stolen. Getting a service back online only shows that it is working again. It does not mean attackers did not copy information before the system was shut down.

Under EU Regulation 2018/1725, a confirmed personal data breach must normally be reported to the European Data Protection Supervisor within 72 hours. If the breach creates a high risk for individuals, they must also be informed without delay. However, these deadlines only start once a personal data breach has been confirmed.

This is not the Commission’s first security incident this year, although no link between the cases has been established. On January 30, attackers left traces in the system used to manage staff mobile devices. Some names and phone numbers were exposed. The Commission said it contained and cleaned up the incident within nine hours.

A more serious incident happened in March. Attackers compromised a software update for Trivy, a security tool, and used it to enter an AWS cloud environment. They stole around 91.7 GB of compressed data, including personal information and email content. The breach may also have affected at least 29 other EU institutions and bodies.

The timeline shows that the Commission restored its systems before it fully understood what had happened. Services came back online in stages, but key questions remain unanswered: where did the attack start, which systems were affected, and was any data stolen, and who is behind the attack?

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, European Commission)

On January 30, attackers left traces in the system used to manage staff mobile devices. Some names and phone numbers were exposed. The Commission said it contained and cleaned up the incident within nine hours.

A more serious incident happened in March. Attackers compromised a software update for Trivy, a security tool, and used it to enter an AWS cloud environment. They stole around 91.7 GB of compressed data, including personal information and email content. The breach may also have affected at least 29 other EU institutions and bodies.

The timeline shows that the Commission restored its systems before it fully understood what had happened. Services came back online in stages, but key questions remain unanswered: where did the attack start, which systems were affected, and was any data stolen, and who is behind the attack?

item.title: U.S. CISA adds Apache Axis, Vanderbilt REDCap,BerriAI LiteLLM, and Synology DSM flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Apache Axis, Vanderbilt REDCap,BerriAI LiteLLM, and Synology DSM flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Check Point and UnrealIRCd vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

  • CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score of 9.8) Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score of 8.8) BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score of 9.8) Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score of 9.8) Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability

The first vulnerability, CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score 9.8), affects Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) and is caused by improper encoding or escaping of output. Synology has confirmed that attackers are exploiting the flaw in ransomware attacks targeting network-attached storage (NAS) devices. The intrusions have resulted in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware, putting data stored on vulnerable devices at risk.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score 8.8), affects BerriAI LiteLLM and is classified as an unprotected alternate channel vulnerability. Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that attackers have exploited it to escalate limited-access inference keys into full administrative credentials. They then established persistence to conduct LLMjacking attacks, abusing compromised AI infrastructure to access large language models. The campaigns targeted organizations in the financial services, retail, transportation and technology sectors across North America, South America and the Asia-Pacific region.

The third vulnerability, CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score 9.8), affects Apache Axis 1.x and involves unsafe reflection. The flaw can allow remote code execution in Atlassian Confluence Data Center when the Remote API feature is enabled. Rapid7 detected attackers exploiting it in a customer environment on November 13, 2026. The threat actors executed shell commands and downloaded scripts through temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains. They then searched the compromised systems for sensitive information, including credentials, tokens, VPN configurations and private keys. The attackers also queried internal services and attempted to obtain additional credentials. Although some of these attempts failed, they managed to acquire a service account credential and access a production cloud data warehouse. They later used the account to sign in to Microsoft 365. Apache Axis 1.x has reached end of life, and no official fix is available for this branch. Organizations should migrate to an alternative SOAP framework or apply the available community patch.

The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score 9.8), affects Vanderbilt University’s Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) platform and is classified as a code injection flaw. Attackers can exploit it through specially crafted HTTP requests that reach an unintended controller route and manipulate file paths or streams during data import operations. Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash. Safe Security observed an unknown threat actor exploiting the vulnerability to deploy a temporary web shell, followed by an in-memory loader that retrieved the XMRig cryptocurrency miner. The attackers disguised the miner as image files and the legitimate syslog-ng process, then established persistence through scheduled tasks and an additional SSH key.

CISA has set remediation deadlines for federal agencies, requiring them to address the Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap vulnerabilities by November 21 or December 2, 2026, depending on the flaw. The active exploitation reports underline the need for organizations to identify exposed systems, apply available fixes or mitigations, and investigate possible signs of compromise.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and REDCap vulnerabilities by November 21 or December 2, 2026, depending on the flaw.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

item.title: Chaotic Eclipse Releases FastUnlock, a New Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability
item.description:
The researcher Chaotic Eclipse released FastUnlock, a new Windows zero-day vulnerability exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare and Nightmare-Eclipse, released a new Windows zero-day vulnerability, dubbed FastUnlock, exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

According to the researcher, exploiting it can bypass BitLocker encryption and allow code execution under the lock screen’s WsiAccount. He claims he breached a fully encrypted Windows 11 26H2 system in just five minutes, even with the November security updates installed.

“It took a total of 5 minutes from finding this to breaching a fully encrypted bitlocker machine with Windows 11 26H2 November Patch installed, an issue caused by total negligence from Microsoft’s side… The vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in, in other words, if you know how to control narrator in the background properly or just press the correct combination of buttons, you will get code execution in the target machine as well.” reads the advisory published by the researcher.

The attack requires physical access to the computer and at least one user account linked to an online account. The researcher says the flaw undermines BitLocker’s protection, which should prevent access to encrypted data even if an attacker has physical access to the device.

He explains that Microsoft introduced the issue while redesigning Narrator, failing to prevent its new interface from running in the lock screen account context. Unlike earlier lock screen bypass flaws, this one is reportedly easier to exploit. The attack can be triggered through the “I forgot my PIN” or password option.

The researcher explains that the attack starts from the Microsoft account recovery screen. Enabling Narrator causes it to focus on a hidden background window. By navigating its options with the keyboard, an attacker can open Narrator’s settings. From there, the researcher says several paths can lead to code execution under the WsiAccount user, including opening File Explorer through the Bluetooth and Devices and AutoPlay settings.

“Now I didn’t show the full code execution demo because I don’t really have a USB stick but I already did this enough times to know what happens next, your next step is to plugin a USB stick, as soon as you do, narrator will focus on explorer showing your mounted storage content and you can just navigate with the same button combination (CAPS LOCK + Arrow keys/Enter/Space), if you do everything properly the binary in your USB stick will be executed in the context of “WsiAccount”” concludes the report. “I have not checked other windows versions so I am not really sure if this might work on windows 10.”

Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports. His releases have mainly targeted Microsoft products, including Windows and Microsoft Defender, with some later exploited in the wild. Among the most notable are the Undefend and RedSun Defender zero-days.

His work has fueled debate over responsible disclosure and the risks of publishing working exploits.

Recently, Chaotic Eclipse revealed that he is Abdelhamid Naceri, a security researcher. Naceri previously worked with Microsoft in the UK and Germany. In a now-deleted X post, he described his departure from the company, claiming Microsoft terminated his employment without giving him a clear reason. He said Microsoft offered several financial settlements, but he rejected them because he wanted a formal explanation and help staying in Germany.

Naceri also said he challenged the dismissal in a German labor court. According to his account, Microsoft changed its arguments during the case, but the court ultimately upheld the termination. He said the long legal dispute left him with almost no compensation and caused serious financial and emotional problems, including treatment in a psychiatric hospital.

The researcher also admitted that an earlier claim that Microsoft had taken legal action against him was fabricated. The claim came during the controversy over Microsoft’s threats of legal action against security researchers who disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.

In September, the researcher released a new zero-day exploit targeting Microsoft Defender. He named the exploit BigDiskBuster, it triggers a Denial of Service Vulnerability in Windows Defender Update.

In the same month, Chaotic Eclipse released multiple zero-day exploits targeting Nvidia (GreenSection) and Microsoft Defender (ShieldCrash).

He also released exploits targeting other anti-malware and defense solutions. Chaotic Eclipse released a zero-day exploit targeting Kaspersky Endpoint Security, which he named HardBreacher, that triggers a privilege escalation flaw. The researcher pointed out that the PoC is unstable and may require repeated attempts, but when successful, it creates a DLL in System32 with full user permissions. The researcher also claims that taking control of Kaspersky’s UI process can disrupt the antivirus and interfere with file-access controls, potentially leaving the system in an unstable state.

The researcher also released a zero-day exploit targeting GenDigital Avast Antivirus, named PrettyPrague. The exploit triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Finally, Chaotic Eclipse released a new zero-day exploit targeting Crowdstrike Falcon cybersecurity platform. The researcher named the exploit FalconFlank, it triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Chaotic Eclipse)

item.title: Hunt.io Uncovers Russian-Speaking Credential Theft Operation Targeting US Banks and Government Accounts
item.description:
Hunt.io uncovered a credential-stealing operation that compromised 603 PCs and exposed bank, government and password manager accounts.

Hunt.io found an exposed open directory sitting on a Netherlands VPS, and inside it was the live loot store of a credential-theft operation. The report describes decrypted password-manager vaults, cleartext bank logins, and accounts behind the federal identity gateways ID.me and Login.gov. No bank or agency was breached directly; this all happened on the victims’ own Windows PCs.


The attackers used three custom-built tools to manage the operation. HavoX handled communication with infected computers and ran commands, Phantom53 managed victims and tasks, while the Kraken Bridge connected the system to an external control panel.

HavoX used encrypted connections and hidden Python scripts to operate quietly. Phantom53 tracked infected devices, while Kraken Bridge sent commands and delivered tasks through temporary download links that were deleted after use.

The operation affected 603 computers, which had been communicating with three command-and-control systems since October 12. In just three weeks, they generated more than 1.2 million connections. At least 57 victims had US bank or government login details stored on their computers, while 46 had accounts linked to federal benefits or identity services. In one case, the attacker cracked an entire LastPass vault offline, recovering 2,880 logins, including access to a bank account, the IRS and the vault’s own sharing key.

The attacker also bypassed Chrome’s newer app-bound encryption by using hardcoded AES-GCM keys for Chrome versions 20 and 21. A script then searched stolen cookies for 28 valuable online services, including Google, Anthropic, Binance, PayPal and several banks.

“Across 16 identified victims, the recovered data contained at least 3,345 decrypted login records from Chrome and Edge databases spanning 15 hosts, including plaintext passwords.” reads the report. “The operators also collected 30 cookie database files and JSON cookie exports from multiple victims.”

Password managers fared no better. LastPass fell to a custom seven-script pipeline that cracked its AES-CBC storage format and pulled 2,880 logins from one vault alone, plus 17 passkeys and secure notes covering Wi-Fi passwords and security answers. 1Password’s master password was cracked for two victims through a PBKDF2, HKDF, and AES-GCM keyset attack, and a developer’s live KeePass database was lifted straight off a GoLand workstation while the app was still open.

Microsoft 365 took a different hit. Stolen ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT session cookies let the operator replay a PKCE OAuth flow and pull live Graph API tokens without ever triggering a login or MFA prompt. Two tenants were confirmed compromised this way, and a reconnaissance log showed the operator mapping accounts and installed software on a corporate host.

The attackers also targeted more than banks and email accounts. Four PowerShell scripts stole session tokens from 35 AI developer tools, including Claude, Codex and Gemini. They also collected credential files, chat histories and API keys. Three other scripts targeted 44 cryptocurrency platforms and seven browser wallet extensions, stealing 6,570 records from 67 victims.

To maintain access to infected computers, the operator used legitimate remote-access tools, including ConnectWise ScreenConnect and Level.io. The Level.io installer was built into the attack platform, allowing the attackers to keep access even after the original malware was removed.

The operator had developed the platform from the ground, and the custom tooling shows it.

The attribution rests on the operator’s own files. Comments, logs, and docstrings across 249 files are written in Russian, in the kind of casual, private language someone uses when they don’t expect anyone else to read it, from a bridge component’s runtime log to section comments inside a seed-phrase search script.

Hunt.io’s defensive advice centers on treating AI CLI credential files the same as SSH keys, enforcing conditional access tied to device state, and alerting on pythonw.exe spawning from unusual locations. None of the affected institutions were hacked, which is itself the point the researchers want understood.

“None of these institutions is breached. What is exposed is live customer access, which is account-takeover fuel.” concludes the report. “The fix sits on the account side: phishing-resistant authentication, session and device binding, and fast resets for the customers in this loot.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Credential Theft Operation)

item.title: Trump’s First Move After the Outages: Fire the Cyber Director
item.description:
Trump fired his national cyber director days after outages hit Microsoft, US flights, and the NSA’s classified network. No link to a cyberattack confirmed.

The White House fired national cyber director Sean Cairncross, a person close to the administration told Reuters. It’s the first major personnel move since a string of tech failures hit the country over the past week. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will take the role temporarily.

The week brought several major disruptions. A global Microsoft outage affected Outlook and Microsoft 365, disrupting services for hundreds of millions of users. A nationwide ground stop also affected more than 18,000 flights. Then, on November 17, the NSA’s classified internal network, NSANet, also went down. CNN reported that six sources confirmed the outage and that some staff at Fort Meade were told to arrive at different times.

Three separate systems experienced major disruptions in less than two weeks, raising questions about what was happening. A Defense Department official said the NSA outage followed routine maintenance and caused a “temporary degradation.” Sources told CNN there was no evidence of a cyberattack. A former senior NSA official explained that NSANet is made up of several interconnected networks with built-in redundancy, making a complete outage unusual. However, by midweek, the agency had not said when all services would be restored.

“The dismissal of Cairncross is the ​administration’s first major personnel move since the outages. Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal ​government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.” Reuters reports.

“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” a person, ​who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.

Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive before taking the cyber director job, said in a statement it had been the honor of a lifetime to serve.

It is important to highlight that nobody has linked these outages to each other or to a foreign actor, at least not officially.

“The top US intelligence official ​said on Wednesday the disruptions ​were separate ⁠service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Reuters continues.

Cybersecurity experts told Reuters separately that the outages are more likely linked to companies rushing to patch vulnerabilities that AI tools now surface faster than before.


This is a plausible explanation, even if it is less appealing than blaming a foreign attacker. Finding vulnerabilities faster means companies need to release security updates more quickly. But faster updates also increase the risk of errors that can disrupt services. A series of outages caused by security measures moving too fast may not make dramatic headlines, but it highlights an important lesson: updates must be properly tested before deployment, even when there is pressure to act quickly.

Not everyone in Washington is satisfied with that account. Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri said this week the administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can tell the public what’s actually happening.

“His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.” Reuters concludes.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – Trump, Cyber Director)

“The dismissal of Cairncross is the ​administration’s first major personnel move since the outages. Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal ​government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.” Reuters reports.

“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” a person, ​who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.

Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive before taking the cyber director job, said in a statement it had been the honor of a lifetime to serve.

It is important to highlight that nobody has linked these outages to each other or to a foreign actor, at least not officially.

“The top US intelligence official ​said on Wednesday the disruptions ​were separate ⁠service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Reuters continues.

Cybersecurity experts told Reuters separately that the outages are more likely linked to companies rushing to patch vulnerabilities that AI tools now surface faster than before.


This is a plausible explanation, even if it is less appealing than blaming a foreign attacker. Finding vulnerabilities faster means companies need to release security updates more quickly. But faster updates also increase the risk of errors that can disrupt services. A series of outages caused by security measures moving too fast may not make dramatic headlines, but it highlights an important lesson: updates must be properly tested before deployment, even when there is pressure to act quickly.

Not everyone in Washington is satisfied with that account. Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri said this week the administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can tell the public what’s actually happening.

“His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.” Reuters concludes.

(SecurityAffairs – Trump, Cyber Director)

item.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Flaw CVE-2026-76466 to Breach Russian Organization (2026)
item.description:
Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 is being exploited to gain root access and move from exposed devices into internal networks.

Attackers have exploited a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8) in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization, and they moved fast once a working exploit went public.

“A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.” reads the advisory.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger the flaw to run commands as root on an affected device. Cisco shipped a fix on 21 October, so this wasn’t a zero-day by the time it got used.


The vulnerability is caused by persistent cookies and weak client certificate checks when TLS Verify Mode is enabled for clustering. An attacker with access to these cookies could connect to the database service and send specific RPC commands, potentially executing arbitrary commands with root privileges on the affected device.

Russian security firm F6 says this is the first known case of the flaw being exploited in the wild, and it happened on Expressway X15.5.3 devices after a proof-of-concept exploit appeared on GitHub. The attackers started with two internet-facing Expressway boxes.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices.” reads the advisory by F6. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.”


The attackers used custom Python scripts to scan networks, find accessible SMB resources, connect to SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories. Their goal was to steal credentials and other sensitive information.

F6’s analysts think AI tools helped write those scripts, judging by the comments and fix descriptions left inside them, which is a strange kind of courtesy from an intruder.

F6 published indicators tied to the activity: two IP addresses, a telltale “[email protected]” entry in the Erlang system log on affected devices, and Python scripts staged under a specific disk path.

“One of the key indicators of successful exploitation is the appearance of a nodeup ‘[email protected]’ entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices.” states F6. “Such an entry indicates that a connection was established with an Erlang node whose identifier corresponds to the known exploitation mechanism — CVE-2026-76466. When such events are detected, organizations should review other logs and artifacts to confirm whether compromise has occurred.”

Nobody has linked the attack to a known group yet, so treat this as an active technique without a named author. If you run Expressway, update now, hunt for those indicators, and don’t assume a clean edge device means a clean network behind it.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Cisco)

item.title: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard Report Third-Party Data Breaches After N0n Claims
item.description:
JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose third-party data breaches after the N0n extortion group claims to have stolen customer information.

The disclosures involving JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard highlight a familiar but often underestimated security problem: the risks introduced by third-party service providers. All three companies have confirmed incidents involving external vendors after the N0n extortion group claimed it had stolen customer information and published data allegedly taken from their systems.

The important distinction is that the companies haven’t reported breaches of their own payment infrastructure. Instead, the incidents appear to involve information held by outside providers, showing how a security failure at a supplier can expose data belonging to major financial institutions and their customers.

JPMorgan said the attackers may have accessed marketing information held by its service providers, including customer names and email addresses.

“Based on our ​investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names ‌and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

The bank stressed that its services weren’t affected and that the incident had no connection to the technical problems some customers experienced earlier in the week. Where necessary, it plans to contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring.

Visa confirmed that the incident it was investigating involved a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company said its own systems hadn’t been affected and that there was no evidence that payment information, including card numbers, had been exposed.

Mastercard also acknowledged a security incident at an external provider. The company said the exposure involved a limited number of email addresses belonging to a small group of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefits program. It stressed that the information wasn’t related to payments and that its payment network remained fully operational.

The N0n group had listed the three companies on its leak site on November 16, claiming to have obtained customer engagement and marketing data. It subsequently published the allegedly stolen information and marked the companies as having refused to pay. The group’s claims should be distinguished from the information independently confirmed by the companies.

The scale of the alleged exposure is significant. According to Reuters’ review, the JPMorgan-related files contained more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some associated with phone numbers and postal codes. Researchers also identified what appeared to be 124 email addresses belonging to bank employees.

The Visa dataset reportedly contained thousands of customer email addresses, phone numbers and marketing campaign records, mainly relating to Asia-Pacific markets. The available information also suggests that the exposure wasn’t limited to customer contact details, although the authenticity and completeness of the files remain important considerations.

Neither JPMorgan, Visa nor Mastercard has identified the affected service providers or disclosed the total number of customers involved. This leaves important questions unanswered, including how attackers accessed the providers’ systems, how long they maintained access and what security controls failed.

Even when attackers don’t obtain card numbers or account credentials, names, email addresses and phone numbers can be valuable. Criminals can use this information to create convincing phishing messages, impersonate financial institutions and target customers with fraudulent calls or messages. A message that includes a person’s name and references a genuine banking relationship is much more likely to attract attention.

For this reason, third-party risk management needs to go beyond contractual security requirements and periodic questionnaires. Organizations should know what information suppliers can access, limit the data they share, review access privileges and require timely incident reporting. They should also verify that providers apply appropriate security controls and have effective procedures to detect and contain intrusions.

The N0n group emerged in September and has listed roughly 200 alleged victims on its leak site. Its claims against the three financial companies show how cyber extortion can affect organizations through their suppliers, even when their core infrastructure and services remain operational.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)
